series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/4] block: do not issue background swap bios as root
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to modify the behavior of bio_issue_as_root_blkg() to not issue background swap bios as root, allowing cgroup IO controllers to throttle such I/O operations. The change is motivated by the need to prevent memory deadlocks in certain scenarios, specifically when using dm-crypt and dm-thin with limit_swap_bios.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with REQ_BACKGROUND marking I/O as not urgent, which could lead to throttling and foreground paging. Suggested reevaluating the patch's design in light of this concern.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> best effort.
> 
> Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> encrypted device").

Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary: Addressed Christoph's concern by clarifying that zswap writebacks are best effort and can tolerate failure, making REQ_BACKGROUND not an issue in this case.
review_comments.raw_body:

On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 11:44 AM Christoph Hellwig <hch@infradead.org> wrote:
>

> On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> > bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> > the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> > swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> > best effort.
> >
> > Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> > for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> > deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> > encrypted device").
>
> Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
> and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
> able to tolerate a failure.
>

Yes, I agree, zswap writebacks are only best effort and in case of
failure, the compressed entry still lives. I don't see how
REQ_BACKGROUND could be an issue there?

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] mm/zswap: turn shrink_memcg_cb()'s argument into a flags word
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `shrink_memcg_cb()` function in the zswap module to accept a flags word instead of a boolean pointer as an argument. The flags word allows callers to pass additional information, specifically whether the walk stopped at an entry already in the swap cache. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather provides a more flexible way for callers to interact with the function. The patch defines a new flag `ZSWAP_SHRINK_SWAPCACHE` and updates the function's logic accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] mm/zswap: allow writeback to be throttled by the cgroup IO controllers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the cgroup IO controllers to throttle zswap writeback operations by introducing a new 'throttled' flag in the swap_io_ctx structure. When this flag is set, the write operation is issued as background I/O instead of being exempt from cgroup throttling, which avoids priority inversion and ensures that memory reclaim is not stalled for other workloads.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] mm/zswap: move reclaim-driven writeback to a kworker
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the reclaim-driven writeback of zswap to a kworker, which writes back data in chunks of SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX entries at a time while holding a reference on the memcg. This change is made to prevent stalls caused by uninterruptible sleeps when the owning cgroup's IO budget is exceeded. The shrinker now reports nothing freed until the worker has run and completed the writeback.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the deferred writeback workers hold a reference on the memcg and requested that queued ones be stopped before calling zswap_memcg_offline_cleanup() to prevent potential issues.

Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the patch introduces a single work item per lruvec on shrink_wq, which may not scale with multiple tasks entering direct reclaim due to idempotent writeback submission, and questioned whether proactive reclaimer and kswapd also need deferred writeback submission.

The reviewer noted that the deferred writeback mechanism will affect the shrinker control loop, causing the accumulation of writebacks to grow over time due to the changed behavior in shrinker_count() and shrinker_scan(), and requested a check be made in do_shrink_slab() in mm/shrinker.c.

Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the patch changes a single-threaded workqueue to a multi-threaded one and suggested adding a mention of this change to the changelog.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 9:23 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:

I understand the problem this patch is trying to solve, but this
solution seems more involved than the changelog suggests :)

---

Ahhh, so it's one work-item (added to the shared shrink_wq)
per-lruvec, not one kworker or thread per-lruvec.

Hmm, supposed multiple tasks in a cgroup enter direct reclaim. In the
past, the amount of writeback submission will scale with the number of
tasks entering reclaim. But now, it's just a single work item
per-lruvec - IIUC, the submission of his work item is idempotent, so
it wouldn't scale like that anymore, right? I haven't wrapped quite
wrapped my head around this, but this sounds like a non-trivial
effect...

Also, do we need to defer writeback submission for proactive
reclaimer? Or kswapd? Only direct reclaimers have concerns with the
latency blowup from the throttling right?

There are a couple more behavioural changes, without proper
justifcation or mentioning in the changelog. More details inlined
below:

---

This will have effect on the shrinker control loop too, right?
Shrinker API accumulates the number of writebacks overtime based on
shrinker_count()'s output, and we serve that number of writebacks
throgh shrinker_scan(). With this basically that accumulation just
grows over time, correct? Check do_shrink_slab() in mm/shrinker.c...

Feels like this completely breaks that control loop.

---

This turns a single-threaded workqueue into multi-threaded workqueue, IIUC.

Worth at least an callout in the changelog?

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the deferred writeback workers hold a reference to the memcg, and requested that queued workers be stopped before calling try_to_unmap() to prevent lock ordering violations.

Reviewer noted that the current implementation may not scale as the number of workers increases, requesting further testing and discussion.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that the writeback bio is issued as root, incurring debt to the cgroup, and with this series throttling the bio at submission, reclaimers would stall on a single cgroup's IO budget; he suggested deferring writeback for everyone.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that the shrinker's behavior needs discussion to prevent zswap from draining 'hot' pages, and suggested clarifying the justifications for all behavioral changes in the next version.

Reviewer noted that while the deferred writeback workers hold a reference to the memcg, they do not drop theirs when they finish, potentially causing issues with reclaim paths.

Reviewer noted that kworker may stall due to exhausting the memcg's IO budget, potentially starving other memcgs, and suggested this as a valid reason for moving writeback to a kworker.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Nhat,

On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 3:43 PM Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com> wrote:

---

It would not scale indeed, the worker does not accumulate in this
version of the patch. That needs to be tested and discussed.

---

Today the writeback bio is issued as root, which incurs debt to the
cgroup. The submitting task repays it on return to user or on any
other IO of the cgroup until the debt is paid off.

With this series the bio is throttled at submission instead, so
whoever submits it sleeps until the cgroup has budget:
- for direct reclaimers, that's the application latency we observed
- for kswapd reclaim, it would stall on a single cgroup's IO budget

So we need to defer for everyone.

---

In the large production workload I have worked on, when the shrinker
is enabled, the zswap pool size decreases by ~97%. So I did not want
to accumulate "too much" work to prevent zswap from draining "hot"
pages, it acts like an additional throttling mechanism. But that needs
discussion, hence the RFC.

And you're right, In the next version, I'll clearly point out all the
behavioral changes I made with their justifications.

---

Yes, this is another behavioural change that I will explain in the next version.

Indeed the work piles up in the shrinker control loop if writeback
cannot catch up but note that it is bounded, which is what we want
right?

---

You're right, and the explanation is "we cannot starve other memcgs if
one worker stalls because it exhausted its memcg budget".

Thanks Nhat!

Alex

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the performance of zswap shrinker on systems running iocost by addressing two issues: (1) zswap writeback is issued as root and charged to the cgroup afterwards, causing stalls in application allocations; and (2) throttled writes sleep in their submitter, often an application thread. The patches modify zswap to mark writebacks as REQ_BACKGROUND instead of REQ_SWAP, allowing them to be throttled by iocost controllers. Additionally, patch 4 moves reclaim-driven writeback to a per-lruvec kworker, reducing the impact on application threads. The series includes benchmarks showing significant performance improvements for various workloads.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern about the scalability of adding multiple kworker threads for zswap writeback, suggesting alternatives such as per-cpu or global threading and inquiring about work accounting from a cgroup perspective.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yeah that tracks with an older experiment of mine, where I add some
manual throttling to zswap shrinker to reduce latency :) So I think
this problem is real - thanks for root-causing this, Alex!

I'm a bit nervous about adding multiple kworker threads though, hmmm.
Per-lruvec sounds like a lot of threads... Do we have to scale this by
lruvec? Why not per-cpu, or just a global thread? Is there any data to
support this autoscaling?

And do we have any concerns with work (CPU) accounting, from a cgroup
perspective...?

review_comments.summary:

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Proposal to introduce more accurate usebackuproot options in Btrfs, including mirroring compression levels and parsing as rescue=usebackuproot[:N]

review_comments.author: Boris Burkov
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about complexity of mirroring compression levels and suggested a simpler approach with 4 options. Approved the current implementation as easier to implement.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary: Responded to Boris' concerns by explaining that the current implementation is simpler and easier to maintain. Provided a brief explanation of why mirroring compression levels was not pursued.
review_comments.raw_body:
在 2026/10/1 03:53, Boris Burkov 写道:
> On Sun, Sep 06, 2026 at 04:33:38PM +0930, Qu Wenruo wrote:
>> Previously we had no way to tell btrfs to use which backup slot, but
>> always use the newest backup, and retry until all backup roots are
>> exhausted.
>>
>> This doesn't give any control to the end user, even if the end user
>> wants to use a specific backup slot.
>>
>> To address this problem, allow more fine-control on usebackuproot rescue
>> option by introducing the following 4 rescue mount options:
>>
>> - rescue=usebackuproot_0
>> - rescue=usebackuproot_1
>> - rescue=usebackuproot_2
>> - rescue=usebackuproot_3
> 
> What do you think about mirroring the compression levels and having the
> option parse as rescue=usebackuproot[:N] rather than 4 options?

That's the solution I tried before, it turns out it's more complex to 
get all the parsing and validation done.

Meanwhile we only need 4 slots to handle, thus this 4 options method is 
surprisingly easier to implement.

Thanks,
Qu

> 
>>
>> The number 0 means the newest slot, which should be the same as the one
>> recorded in the super block and no need to load any backup root.
>>
>> 1/2/3 means the second/third/fourth(oldest) backup slot to use.
>>
>> The existing "rescue=usebackuproot" is just an alias of

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v4 0/7] sched/numa: stop VMA scan filters from gating promotion

version_history.subject: [PATCH v4 0/7] sched/numa: stop VMA scan filters from gating promotion

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mode for NUMA hinting scans that only promotes pages to higher tiers without scanning the entire VMA. The global balancing mode is used to determine the intent of an individual protection walk, and the patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY to select this promotion-only mode. The change-protection flags are built in task_numa_work() based on the balancing mode, and folio_can_map_prot_numa() derives the single-threaded private state at the point of use instead of adding another precomputed boolean to the protection-walk interface. This patch is required for memory-tiering fixes and must be accompanied by them when backported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows shared copy-on-write folios and executable file folios mapped by multiple processes to be promoted from slow memory to a faster tier, as long as the migration is from south to north. This change enables promotion for low-tier folios to top-tier, but maintains existing restrictions for ordinary placement and non-promotion migrations. The patch also renames the `folio_use_access_time` function to `folio_numab_promotable` to better reflect its purpose.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA balancing code to scan read-only file mappings when tiering is enabled, but only performs promotion scans on these mappings. This change allows hot file folios on slow memory to be promoted to faster memory, preventing them from getting stuck in slower memory. The patch also retains the existing restriction of excluding shared libraries from migration. With this change, binary tier residency can track runtime hotness more accurately.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the logic of VMA placement from scan continuation in the Linux kernel's scheduling and NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) code. The existing `vma_is_accessed` function returned true for both placement eligibility and scan progress, which made it difficult to distinguish between these two states. The patch introduces a new function `vma_needs_placement_scan` that handles placement eligibility, while the `task_numa_work` function is modified to handle scan continuation state. This separation allows PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned for promotion without treating scan continuation as evidence of placement eligibility, which is a prerequisite for a subsequent fix.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) memory management to bypass a filter that suppresses faults needed to promote hot slow-tier memory. The filter, which skips VMAs without recent PID activity, is disabled for promotion-only scans and only enabled when a VMA scan starts. This change allows for more efficient scanning of large VMAs and reduces the risk of starving in-progress placement scans. The patch also introduces a new field to track the last completed placement scan separately from other scans. With this modification, memory tiering can adapt to changing workloads and improve system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 6/7] mm: use BIT() for change_protection() flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the MM_CP_* flags in include/linux/mm.h to use the BIT() macro consistently, replacing open-coded shifts. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve code readability and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 7/7] mm: use VMA flag helpers in NUMA balancing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NUMA balancing code in the Linux kernel to use VMA flag helpers instead of directly accessing vm_flags. This change is made to improve code readability and maintainability by encapsulating the logic for checking specific flags within the VMA structure. The existing flag predicates remain unchanged, and no functional changes are intended. The patch applies to three files: kernel/sched/fair.c, mm/internal.h, and mm/migrate.c.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses poor NUMA balancing behavior in a production deployment by stopping VMA scan filters from gating memory-tier promotion. The issue arises because the global balancing mode cannot describe the intent of an individual VMA/PTE walk (placement vs promotion). To fix this, the patch plumbs scan reasoning into the prot_none injection while retaining placement-scan filtering. It introduces promotion-only NUMA protection walks and derives private VMA state in the folio eligibility check. The patches also separate VMA placement eligibility from partial-scan continuation and scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion. Additionally, it uses BIT() for change_protection flags and the VMA flag API in touched NUMA-balancing code.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] mm/numa_balancing: allow migrate on protnone reference with MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE policy
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch proposes to allow migration of pages on protnone reference with MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE policy, aiming to improve initial faulting placement and reduce hot memory consolidation.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's justification and suggested that userspace could set weighted interleave initially using set_mempolicy() or mbind().

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Proposed an alternative solution where userspace can switch to numa balancing via set_mempolicy() or mbind() after a certain threshold is met.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 30 Sep 2026, at 10:50, Gregory Price wrote:

> On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 10:02:23PM +0800, Li Zhe wrote:
>> The use case is closer to the second one, but the main motivation is not
>> only startup-time performance. The more important point is that each
>> workload has its own DDR/CXL budget assigned by the workload manager.
>>
>
> mempolicy is the wrong interface to do budget policy, you'd be better
> off looking at Joshua's memcg tiered node solutions for that.
>
>> MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE is useful because it lets new allocations
>> follow that per-workload budget from the beginning, instead of placing
>> everything on one tier first and correcting the placement later. This is
>> important for workload orchestration because the workload starts from a
>> placement close to its assigned DDR/CXL ratio.
>>
>
> This however is reasonable to me - you'd prefer to spread out the cost
> of initial faulting placement explicitly, rather than simply take
> fallbacks when the top-tier budget becomes pressured.
>
> i.e. w/o interleave:
>
> [node 0       ]
> ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ alloc until full
>                 vvvvvvvvv fallback
>                 [node 1          ]
>
> in this scenario you end up with considerable hot memory
> on the remote node consolidated in time-space (everything
> allocated after node0 becomes full skews heavily toward
> node1)
>
> Tiering then likely takes many faults to rebalance after
> you've already reached node0 limits.
>
> w/ interleave
>
> [node 0                                      ]
>  ^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv^^^vv....
> [node 1                                      ]
>
> In this scenario you do an initial fill distributed by weight
> and then let tiering figure it out without consolidating all
> of the pressure to the point where node0 has no space left.
>
> That said - this seems like mostly an initial-fill problem, after
> you initially fill your memory, a new allocation largely implies
> the memory is hot - and you probably prefer that to be local.

If this is a initial-fill problem, can userspace set weighted interleave
initially? The program or harness can observe memory usage of the program
or related NUMA nodes and switch the policy to numa balancing via
set_mempolicy() or mbind() without MPOL_MF_MOVE after certain threshold
is met?



Best Regards,
Yan, Zi

> (weighted when mechanism A honors them and mechanism B doesn't honor them), but
> once we set these semantics in stone like that, we cannot easily change them
> later because some user might depend on that behavior.
> 
> So you'll need yet another flag to say "NUMA balancing really also honors the
> weights". And that's where it all gets ugly.
> 

I would agree with you if demotion didn't entirely ignoring mempolicy.

On a tiered system, mempolicy *only* applies to initial (or fault-in)
placement, and otherwise is more or less entirely ignored.  This is
a case where it's not ignored - which is actually inconsistent with
the rest of the tiering tools (demotion, damon).

This is why I said this distinction may only make sense in TIERING
mode, while in NORMAL mode you likely just want to fault it back to
its original interleave location.

Also file interleave (indexed by offset) vs task (counter-incremented)
policies are affected by these changes very differently, which I asked
for some thought on.

As tiering develops, the less I think task-mempolicy as a whole makes
much sense (because it's at-best advisory).

~Gregory

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch removes a limitation in the NUMA balancing code that prevents migration of pages when the policy has MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE set and there is no preferred node (protnone reference). The change allows for more flexible page placement, potentially improving performance by enabling NUMA balancing to optimize placement among multiple nodes.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: reviewer suggested consolidating MPOL_F_MORON check into a single generic path at the top, eliminating redundant checks and simplifying exit paths
review_comments.raw_body:
+1, I like this idea, especialy since the switch-case break case already
leads to an MPOL_F_MORON check at the bottom. It would be nice to just
consolidate this into one generic path at the top and simplify the
exit path as well.

review_comments.author: Li Zhe
review_comments.summary: reviewer suggested reordering the logic to handle MPOL_F_MORON before policy-specific cases, allowing for a shared migrate-on-fault path among policies that opt in to this behavior
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, that makes sense to me.

I do not see a reason to keep the MPOL_F_MORON handling limited to
specific policy cases. The flag already means that migrate-on-fault
placement should target the accessing CPU's node, and the nodemask check
is the common constraint we want for all policies that opt in to this
behavior.

I will rework v2 to handle MPOL_F_MORON before the policy-specific
switch. Then the switch can remain responsible for the non-MPOL_F_MORON
misplaced logic, while MPOL_BIND, MPOL_PREFERRED_MANY, MPOL_INTERLEAVE
and MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE can share the same migrate-on-fault path.

Thanks,
Zhe

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged Li Zhe's suggestion to remove the F_MORON check and instead proposed breaking up the change into separate parts, considering different behavior for task-mempolicy and vma-mempolicy, and limiting the change based on NUMA balancing mode. No fix is planned in this response.
review_comments.raw_body:
I do think it's worth breaking this up a bit, we can decide whether we
want to apply it to interleave separate of the larger change.

there is also slightly different behavior for task-mempolicy and
vma-mempolicy, because vma-mempolicy applies interleave via index while
task mempolicy does it based on a rolling counter, so you'll want to
think about what happens on repeated faults

i.e.

1) fault in a VMA interleaved based on idx
2) a bunch of tiering and pageout/swap happens
3) we fault a page back in based on idx - that means this page is
   forever-faulted onto that location rather than taking that as an
   indication that maybe it should be local

Maybe we're ok with that, but we should probably think about it a bit.

We may also want to limit this based on NUMA balancing being in tiering
mode vs normal mode.  This only makes sense in tiering mode, in my
opinion.  In normal mode i'm not sure it makes as much sense - and
that's probably where this all came from.

tl;dr: If we want to change this behavior for interleave, we should
probably give more thought for how it should apply more generally
instead of just hacking on support to one or two modes.

~Gregory

Zhe

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] sched/psi: clamp negative cpu_clock() skew
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch aims to clamp negative cpu_clock() skew, but reviewers raise concerns about the implementation and its impact on x86 architecture.

review_comments.author: David Stevens
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with rdtsc() producing non-monotonic results on x86, which could explain the negative skew. Suggested adding a rbm() to match the behavior of rdtsc_ordered().
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 8:19 AM Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org> wrote:
>
> On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 10:22:52AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> > On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 10:17:40AM +0200, Peter Zijlstra wrote:
> > > On Tue, Sep 29, 2026 at 10:10:04AM +0200, Peter Zijlstra wrote:
> > >
> > > > > When running browser workloads on an Intel N100 with a sustained
> > > > > psi.mem.some of 2-3%, this underflow is observed once every couple of
> > > > > hours.
> > >
> > > Reading is hard. This is sad, that's a relatively modern chip :-(
> >
> > I'm still struggling, but I'm under the weather so bear with me.
> >
> > That's a cpu_clock() implementation issue, right? "The value for
> > cpu_clock(i) is monotonic for constant i". Presumably violating that
> > would be a problem beyond psi?
>
> Yeah, although most everybody has a filter on top for some reason or
> another.
>
> Mostly it could happen that when the watchdog would detect the TSC
> wasn't stable after all, you'd be up a creek if you didn't also have
> this filter.
>
> But I'm very sad to see modern chips have shit TSC, that wasn't supposed
> to happen.

I ran artificial memory pressure tests on the other two devices I have
at hand - one with an Intel i5-1245U and one with an Intel Ultra 5
325. Both devices also observed negative elapsed durations. The
artificial workloads were much heavier and actually produced negative
elapsed durations every couple of minutes. So this doesn't look like a
platform-specific issue.

For reference, the negative elapsed durations I saw averaged a little
under 100ns. The largest duration I saw was 371ns.

If I'm following the code correctly, cpu_clock() on x86 ends up
calling rdtsc() via sched_clock(). The rdtsc() function is documented
to produce non-monotonic results when compared across CPUs, since the
rdtsc instruction can read the tsc out of order relative to other
instructions. If that results in get_recent_times() reading the tsc
before it reads the psi state, then I think that would explain the
negative skew. I added a rbm() immediately before the call to
cpu_clock() in get_recent_times() to match the behavior of
rdtsc_ordered(), and with that I didn't see any negative elapsed
durations during overnight testing. This does suggest that calling
through to sched_clock() might not provide strong enough guarantees on
x86 to satisfy the cpu_clock() contract.

-David

version_history.subject: [PATCH 7.2.y] selftests/cgroup: account for zswap shrinker writeback

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/cgroup test to account for zswap shrinker writeback when checking if a cgroup triggers writeback for other cgroups. The test previously checked that the victim cgroup had zero writebacks, but this could lead to probabilistic failures due to delayed writebacks. Instead, the patch compares the writeback values before and after the aggressor runs and checks that the victim cgroup did not perform any additional writeback. This should fix systematic failure cases and make test failures less likely.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of page allocation in defrag_mode to make retries follow the promoted order, rather than the original request order. This change is intended to prevent indefinite retrying by requests that are not movable, which can lead to reclaim storms and excessive memory pressure. The patch treats promoted requests as costly orders, resetting progress counters for them and checking compaction results at the promoted order. It also resets retry counters when a fallback attempt is taken, allowing it to get a full retry budget before the OOM killer is considered. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory pressure in systems with high inode churn under memory.low protection.

review_comments.author: Harry Yoo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Harry Yoo suggested that the patch should distinguish between order and compact/reclaim_order in __alloc_pages_slowpath() to improve code readability and prevent mistakes.

Reviewer Harry Yoo questioned the logic of changing how hard direct compaction tries to compact in defrag_mode, suggesting it doesn't align with the rest of the patch
review_comments.raw_body:
I think we should start distinguishing order and compact/reclaim_order
in __alloc_pages_slowpath(). Silently overriding it makes it harder to
follow and easy to make a mistake.

This would change how hard we try to compact with defrag_mode in direct
compaction as it won't try compaction with MIN_COMPACT_PRIORITY anymore.

It doesn't make much sense to change that as part of this fix?

The author is responding to a request from Andrew Morton to make defrag mode the default, citing its importance for using large folios in page cache and noting that only they test it.

crucial if we want to use large folios in page cache.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author agreed that four callers recomputing the same promoted order is inefficient, but prefers not to grow this patch and plans a separate cleanup in v2.

Author acknowledges that promoting order-0 requests to pageblock can trigger SYNC_FULL compaction, and is willing to try it out with the reproducer.
review_comments.raw_body:
Agreed, four callers recomputing the same thing is asking for a
mismatch.

I would rather not grow this patch, it has to go to stable.

I will look into a cleanup on top: __alloc_pages_slowpath() computes the
promoted order once per iteration and passes it to direct
reclaim/compaction and the two retry helpers next to the request order,
so the helpers stop knowing about defrag_mode.

---

It is a choice between compacting harder and falling back, which
fragments a block.

It is a judgement call on what defrag_mode means.

It would also mean that order-0 allocation request promoted to pageblock
can trigger SYNC_FULL compaction. I cannot say I understand the
implications. Will give it a try with the reproducer.

Johannes, Vlastimil, any comments here?

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer noted that despite fixing the original issue of an allocating thread spinning on a goal it doesn't help accomplish, the new patch still causes the thread to spin and help, but the goal is not achievable, indicating that the problem has been shifted rather than solved.

The reviewer suggests simplifying the patch by focusing on the distinction between requested and production orders (reclaim_order and compaction_order) rather than introducing new variables.

Reviewer Johannes Weiner expressed concerns that the patch may inadvertently create a self-defeating scenario in defrag_mode by allowing fallbacks too easily, potentially making it harder to compact towards higher bars over time.
sentiment_signals: raising the bar for fallbacks not high enough
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for fixing this. Ironically, the same workload blowing up again
that I tested the old fix again for 3 weeks :(

Back then, the problem was: allocating thread is spinning on a goal it
doesn't help accomplish.

Now the problem is: allocating thread spinning and helping, but goal
is not achievable.

---

+1

All they really need to know is the split into requested order vs
production order (reclaim_order, compaction_order).

---

I would leave this one with requested order unless the reproducer
disagrees.

There is a risk of defrag_mode self defeating over time by raising the
bar for fallbacks but not high enough. Every fallback we let through
will make it harder down the line to compact towards that higher bar.

There is also a non-zero risk of connecting order-0 request contexts
to SYNC compaction which they haven't done before 7e8756d7ad22. But
you traced the problem to retrying, not sync compaction itself.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order
